person: Carmen Ruiz, 44, is the entire HR department at a 46-person metal-fabrication plant in upstate New York. She came up from payroll clerk and now handles benefits and, by default, the workers' comp audit, which she reports to the CFO and to an outside employment lawyer who bills by the quarter hour. The carrier's auditor has put several office and sales people into shop classes, taken no credit for overtime premium on one shift, and counted two subcontractors' costs as uninsured payroll. She wants each dispute tied to a rule and a record before anything goes to the carrier, and she will approve every submission herself. She keeps the dispute deadline on her paper calendar.
stated_up_front: The carrier's audit came back with a much higher premium than we expected and I think some lines are wrong. Can you go through the auditor's worksheet against our payroll records and contracts and tell me which ones we can dispute, with the rule for each? Don't send anything to the carrier until I've okayed it.

facts.truth: The carrier's audit notice says disputes must be in by 6 November 2026; Carmen has it circled on her paper calendar.

Dana Whitfield, about $52,000 a year, is classed in the machine shop code. Her time records show she works at her desk in the front office all 40 hours and never goes onto the floor. She should be clerical.

Luis Ortega, about $78,000 a year, visits customers' plants and works from home or on the road. The auditor put him in the shop class. His time records show no hours at the plant beyond a weekly sales meeting.
The Payroll Harbor register for the second-shift cell records overtime premium as a separate line, about $18,400 for the year. The extra half of that should come off the audited payroll.
The first-shift register lumps overtime into regular wages with no separate premium line, so no exclusion can be claimed there.

facts.about: Production planner who walks the floor
facts.truth: Marcus Hale, the production planner, has a desk title but his time records show about 22 hours a week on the shop floor. Carmen accepts he stays in the shop class.

Hudson Valley Rigging, $31,500 for the year, has a workers' comp certificate on file with the BrokerLink agent covering the dates it worked. Calloway Electric, $12,800, has a workers' comp certificate stapled only in its SharePoint contract file, also in force for the dates it worked.

A freight hauler, Tri-County Trucking, has only a general-liability certificate. A landscaper, Greenline, has a workers' comp policy that expired in March, before it worked in June. Both stay in the premium.
A recovery firm called AuditBack emailed offering to fight the audit for 40 percent of whatever is returned. Carmen intends to decline it and do the disputes herself.
The prior year's audit closed in August 2026, and the carrier's dispute window for it ended on 30 September.

unknowns: Which manual rule or section decides each class question; Carmen knows the outcomes but not the rule numbers.
Whether the carrier will allow a late dispute on last year's audit.
Whether the agent's certificate for Calloway Electric will be accepted when the agent's own file does not hold it.
What the class codes on the auditor's worksheet mean.
